screens.title: Working with Light Probes and Reflection Probes
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we'll learn why Light Probes and Reflection Probes are essential when you combine baked environments with dynamic objects. Light Probes sample baked indirect lighting at points in space so moving characters and props receive smooth ambient illumination and color bounces. Reflection Probes capture panoramic cubemaps so metallic, glass, or water materials show believable reflections from their surroundings. You'll see placement strategies, when to bake, and which probe types to choose for different performance budgets. We’ll also practice creating a Light Probe Group, spreading probes across doorways, corners, and heights, and then baking so dynamic renderers blend nearby probe data. For reflections we’ll compare baked and realtime probes, set influence volumes and resolution, and use blend distances to avoid abrupt transitions. This knowledge matters because correctly configured probes preserve realism without the cost of full realtime global illumination. By the end of the chapter you’ll be able to place and tune probes to get natural-looking dynamic objects and accurate reflections, and avoid common pitfalls like probes inside geometry or a single oversized probe for complex rooms. Ready to explore probe techniques and hands-on steps that you can apply in your next scene?

Working with Light Probes and Reflection Probes

Learn how to make dynamic objects receive baked indirect light and believable reflections, while keeping performance and visual accuracy balanced.

Orientation

We first explain what probes sample, then how to place them, bake lighting, and finally how to tune reflections and blending. Practical steps and common mistakes are included.

Bake

Reflection Types
Use baked probes for static rooms, realtime for special dynamic cases, or custom cubemaps where needed.

screens.title: What Light Probes Do
screens.narratorSegment: Light Probes are invisible sample points that capture the baked indirect light at a position so dynamic objects can receive believable ambient illumination. In concrete terms, Unity stores a small set of lighting coefficients at each probe. When a dynamic mesh moves through the scene, Unity interpolates the lighting from the nearest probes to determine the indirect diffuse contribution applied to that mesh. For example, if your character walks from a warm-lit corridor into a cooler shadowed room, properly placed probes ensure the character picks up the warm orange tint near the corridor and the softer blue-gray in the room. A common misconception is that Light Probes provide full, per-pixel global illumination for dynamic objects. They do not; probes provide an interpolated ambient sample, not full GI. Another mistake is treating probes like geometry: never place them inside walls or inside floors, because they sample from their local open space. To use probes, create a Light Probe Group, edit its probe positions at varying heights and near surfaces, and re-bake lighting so each probe stores the correct indirect data. Key takeaway: Light Probes bridge baked static lighting and dynamic objects with lightweight interpolated samples, preserving the visual connection between moving and static elements without realtime GI cost. How might you change probe density when a character can jump between floors?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Light Probes sample baked indirect light to provide interpolated ambient lighting for dynamic objects.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › What Light Probes Do
Definition

Light Probes are spatial sample points that store baked indirect lighting so dynamic objects can receive interpolated ambient illumination matching the environment.

Why they matter
Without probes, dynamic objects in a baked scene look flat because they lack the indirect light and color bounces that static objects show.
Concrete example
A player walking from a warm corridor into a cool room will inherit the corridor's warm tint near the doorway if probes are placed across the transition.
Common mistake
Placing probes inside geometry or too few probes over a transition causes popping or abrupt lighting changes on dynamic objects.
Key Takeaway

Light Probes are a low-cost way to carry baked indirect illumination to moving objects, but they require deliberate placement and rebaking to be effective.

Probe visualization & usage
A Light Probe Group starts as a small grid. You can select and move individual probes, duplicate them, and build coverage where dynamic objects travel. Remember to rebake lighting after adjustments so probes store updated samples.
Placement tip
Place probes at varying heights to capture vertical light differences when characters jump or climb.
Surface proximity
Place probes near colored walls or floors to capture color bounces that affect object tint.
Check your understanding
If a dynamic prop looks flat in a baked room, ask whether probes are present and whether the Mesh Renderer is set to Blend Probes.

screens.title: Creating and Placing a Light Probe Group
screens.narratorSegment: Creating an effective Light Probe Group is a deliberate process: create the group, edit probes, place them to cover expected dynamic movement, and rebake lighting so probes store the sampled data. Start by adding a Light Probe Group, which provides an initial grid you can edit. Enter the probe edit mode and move individual probes: spread them near doorways, in corners, and at differing heights to capture vertical variations. A useful rule of thumb is to place probes near surfaces that contribute color bounces, like a red wall or glossy floor, and to ensure probes sit in open space rather than inside mesh. Duplicate probes to extend coverage along expected paths. After placement, generate lighting so the probes capture baked indirect light. Watch the results by moving a non-static object through the scene. If you see abrupt lighting shifts, add probes near the problematic transition rather than increasing probe density uniformly. A common misconception is that more probes always equal better results; instead, focus probes where lighting changes and use fewer probes in uniform areas to balance memory and bake time. This workflow helps you achieve smooth lighting interpolation while keeping resource use reasonable.

keyIdea.title: Step-by-step
keyIdea.text: Edit a Light Probe Group: position probes at transitions and heights, duplicate as needed, then rebake to capture sampled indirect lighting.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Creating Light Probe Group
Process: Create → Edit → Bake
  1. Create a Light Probe Group in the scene.
  2. Edit probe positions: spread near doorways, corners, and at varying heights.
  3. Duplicate probes to extend coverage along likely paths.
  4. Bake lighting so probes sample the indirect illumination.
  5. Validate by moving a dynamic object and watching for smooth transitions.
Placement mnemonic
Think "Heights, Edges, Surfaces, Open Space" — capture vertical change, transitions, surface color bounces, and keep probes out of geometry.
Placement examples
Near doorway: place probes on both sides to capture differing room bounces.
At varying heights: capture lighting when characters crouch or jump.
Adjacent to colored walls: capture tint for more accurate object coloration.
Common mistake
Placing probes inside geometry or using an even grid without considering movement paths leads to poor interpolation and visible popping.

screens.title: Editing, Duplicating, and Baking Probes
screens.narratorSegment: After placing initial probes you’ll refine coverage by selecting individual probes, moving them, or duplicating to fill gaps. Use the engine’s edit mode to pick specific probes and nudge them near surfaces or along movement paths. When refining, ask whether additional probes solve localized transitions or whether their benefit would be marginal; add probes only where lighting changes noticeably. Once satisfied with placement, rebake your lighting. Baking is crucial: Light Probes do not automatically sample updated indirect light until you generate lighting, so a common error is changing probe positions and forgetting to bake, which leaves probes with stale samples. For verification, place a non-static test object — for instance a capsule or player rig — and move it across probe regions. Observe subtle color shifts and brightness changes. If lighting pops, inspect probe placement near the popping boundary and add a probe to smooth interpolation. Keep balance in mind: too many probes increase memory and bake time, too few cause artifacts. The final step is to ensure the dynamic object's Mesh Renderer uses Blend Probes so it will interpolate the nearby probe data automatically. What small change could you make if your test object still looks too flat after rebaking?

keyIdea.title: Bake workflow
keyIdea.text: Edit probes, duplicate as needed, then rebake lighting so probes capture accurate samples; validate by moving a dynamic object through the scene.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Editing & Baking Probes
Edit and duplicate probes
Select probes in edit mode, move them near surfaces, change heights, and duplicate to fill gaps along movement paths.
Tip
Use duplication to extend probe coverage quickly along a corridor or stairwell while keeping spacing consistent.
Validation
Move a capsule or player object through the area after rebaking to inspect interpolation and detect popping.
Bake lighting
After every meaningful placement change, generate lighting so probes obtain fresh baked samples. Probes only store samples after a bake.
Common mistake
Forgetting to rebake leaves probes with old data and gives the illusion that probes are broken.
Check
Confirm the Mesh Renderer on dynamics is set to Blend Probes so they use interpolated data automatically.
Key Takeaway

Edit probes, rebake, and validate with dynamic objects. Add probes where lighting transitions occur rather than uniformly increasing density.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Balancing Probe Count
screens.narratorSegment: A frequent challenge is balancing probe count against memory and bake-time cost. Too few probes cause visible popping and abrupt lighting changes on dynamic objects. Too many probes increase memory usage and lengthen bake times without a proportionate visual gain. Compare two approaches: a sparse uniform grid versus targeted placement. A sparse grid may miss transitions and color bounces, while targeted placement focuses probes at doorways, corners, and heights where dynamic objects move. A common misconception is that simply increasing total probes across the whole scene will always improve result; instead, prioritise probes where lighting changes. Another mistake is placing probes inside geometry or embedded in meshes; probes must sit in open space to sample the correct ambient light. For reflections, many artists try using a single large Reflection Probe for a big scene; this produces parallax errors and inaccurate reflections far from the probe center. Better is multiple smaller probes with overlapping blend distances to localize reflections and maintain geometric plausibility. The right balance keeps visuals realistic while controlling resource cost. Ask yourself: where does the player actually move, and where will reflections and light transitions be noticed most?

keyIdea.text: Place probes where they affect perceived lighting most; avoid probe overuse and never embed probes inside geometry.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Mistakes & Balancing
Too few probes

Leads to abrupt lighting transitions and popping on dynamic objects. Add probes specifically at transitions rather than applying a uniform grid everywhere.

Symptom
Character lighting suddenly changes when crossing an uncovered threshold.
Too many probes

Raises memory and bake time for diminishing returns. Focus probes where they change perception, not everywhere.

Symptom
Longer bakes and larger lighting data but marginal visual improvements in uniform areas.
Reflection probe note
Avoid a single large reflection probe for a complex room. Use multiple localized probes with blend distances to correct parallax and keep reflections geometrically plausible.

screens.title: What Reflection Probes Capture
screens.narratorSegment: Reflection Probes capture a panoramic snapshot of a point in your scene and store that environment as a cubemap texture. That cubemap is then sampled by reflective materials to show environment reflections that match the local surroundings. Reflection Probes are essential for metallic surfaces, glossy plastics, water, and glass. There are three common probe types: baked, realtime, and custom. Baked probes capture a static cubemap during the lighting bake and are typically used for interiors where the environment doesn't change. Realtime probes update dynamically and can reflect moving objects or changing skies, but they are expensive and should be used sparingly. Custom probes let you assign a pre-made cubemap. Another key concept is the influence volume: the probe only affects objects within its box size and offset. When multiple probes overlap, use blend distance to smooth transitions so reflections change gradually between probe regions. A typical mistake is relying on a single probe for a large, complex area — this yields inaccurate parallax and unrealistic reflections far from the probe center. The correct approach is to localize probes and control blend distances so reflections remain convincing.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Reflection Probes capture cubemaps used by reflective materials; their influence volumes define where those reflections apply.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Reflection Probes
What they store

A Reflection Probe captures a cubemap — six square faces representing the surrounding environment — which reflective materials sample to produce reflections.

Types
Baked, Realtime, or Custom cubemaps depending on whether reflections must update dynamically.
Influence
Box Size and Offset define the influence volume where the probe's cubemap applies to objects.
Key Takeaway

Use baked probes for static interiors and realtime probes only for special dynamic reflections due to cost. Localize probes and use blending for smooth results.

Concrete example
Place a baked probe at room center with resolution 128–256, set box size to encompass the room, and bake. A metallic sphere in that room will then reflect the stored cubemap and show room features instead of a generic skybox.
Resolution
Higher resolution gives sharper reflections at a cost to texture memory.
Blend Distance
Smooths transitions when probes overlap so reflections change gradually.
Misconception
Realtime probes automatically fix everything. They are costly and do not fix parallax errors if used as a single large probe for a big area.

screens.title: Reflection Probe Properties and Trade-offs
screens.narratorSegment: Reflection Probes come with several properties you must tune deliberately. Type determines how the cubemap is produced: Baked captures a static snapshot during the lighting bake and is the usual choice for static interiors. Realtime updates frames or at intervals and is reserved for special cases like mirrors or dynamic vehicles because it has a high runtime cost. Custom allows assignment of an authored cubemap. Resolution sets cubemap sharpness: higher resolution yields crisper reflections but consumes texture memory and increases bake or generation time. Box Size and Box Offset define the probe's influence volume — objects within that box sample the probe; objects outside do not. If probes overlap, Blend Distance smooths the transition so reflections interpolate rather than switch abruptly. For Realtime probes the Refresh Mode controls when cubemaps update, for example every frame or only on specific events; choose lower-frequency refreshes to save performance. A typical approach is to use baked probes per room with resolution around 128–256, and add smaller probes for specific reflective hotspots. Ask: does the visual improvement justify the memory and performance cost of a higher-resolution or realtime probe?

keyIdea.text: Tune probe type, resolution, and influence volume to balance reflection fidelity and performance; prefer baked probes for static scenes.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Probe Properties
Key properties
Type: Baked, Realtime, Custom — choose based on dynamic needs and performance.
Resolution: Controls sharpness of reflections — higher uses more memory.
Box Size / Offset: Defines where the probe influences objects.
Refresh Mode: For realtime probes, select update frequency to trade accuracy for cost.
Practical guideline
Start with baked probes per room at 128–256 resolution. Add smaller probes for reflective hotspots and use blend distances to smooth overlaps.
Concrete example
For an interior room, place a baked probe at center, set box size to encompass the room, resolution to 128 for a good balance, and bake. For a mirror or dynamic reflective object, consider a small realtime probe with limited refresh rate or a custom cubemap for predictable results.
Misconception
Higher resolution or realtime updates will not fix a probe placed far from the object; localization matters more than raw resolution.

screens.title: Placement Strategies and Blend Distance
screens.narratorSegment: Good reflection placement is about localization and smooth blending. Place a reflection probe where reflections matter most — the center of a room, near water, or close to clusters of metallic objects. For large, complex rooms, distribute multiple smaller probes rather than a single large one; this avoids parallax errors where reflections appear geometrically wrong far from the probe center. When probe volumes overlap, use Blend Distance to interpolate between their cubemaps, creating a smooth transition. Too small a blend distance causes abrupt reflection changes; too large may blur localized detail. A practical sequence: place probes to cover each distinct sub-region, set box sizes to cover the relevant surfaces, then adjust blend distances to smooth transition zones like doorways. Validate by moving a reflective object across the overlap and noting whether reflections change gradually. A frequent misconception is that perfect geometric parallax requires realtime cubemaps; often, well-placed baked probes with smart blending give convincing results at lower cost. In short: localize, overlap thoughtfully, and fine-tune blend distance to maintain both realism and performance. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Placement & Blending
Where to place probes
Per room center, near water, at reflective clusters, and around doorways. Localized probes reduce parallax artifacts.
Overlap strategy
Place probes with overlapping boxes and use blend distance to create smooth changes between them.
Validation
Move a reflective sphere across an overlap and look for gradual changes rather than abrupt jumps.
Blend distance tuning
Start small and increase until the reflection transition looks natural. Balance sharpness and smoothness for each overlap zone.
Practical example
Two probes in adjacent rooms: set blend distance across the doorway to soften the reflection switch as an object moves between rooms.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Hands-on Activity
Activity summary
Integrate Light Probe Group and Reflection Probe in a baked interior. Use test dynamic objects to validate lighting and reflections after baking.
Step-by-step
  1. Prepare a baked interior scene. Add a non-static Sphere (metallic) and Capsule as dynamic objects.
  2. Create a Light Probe Group. Enter edit mode and position probes near corners, doorways, and at varying heights.
  3. Duplicate probes along paths where dynamics will move. Ensure probes are not inside geometry.
  4. Generate lighting so probes capture indirect light samples.
  5. Add a Reflection Probe at the room center. Set Type to Baked and Resolution to 128–256. Adjust Box Size to cover the room.
  6. Bake reflections. Move the metallic sphere and observe localized reflections. Add a second probe and set Blend Distance if transitions need smoothing.
Pro-tip
When testing, move objects slowly across probe boundaries to spot popping and tune probe positions or blend distances accordingly.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we'll learn why Light Probes and Reflection Probes are essential when you combine baked environments with dynamic objects. Light Probes sample baked indirect lighting at points in space so moving characters and props receive smooth ambient illumination and color bounces. Reflection Probes capture panoramic cubemaps so metallic, glass, or water materials show believable reflections from their surroundings. You'll see placement strategies, when to bake, and which probe types to choose for different performance budgets. We’ll also practice creating a Light Probe Group, spreading probes across doorways, corners, and heights, and then baking so dynamic renderers blend nearby probe data. For reflections we’ll compare baked and realtime probes, set influence volumes and resolution, and use blend distances to avoid abrupt transitions. This knowledge matters because correctly configured probes preserve realism without the cost of full realtime global illumination. By the end of the chapter you’ll be able to place and tune probes to get natural-looking dynamic objects and accurate reflections, and avoid common pitfalls like probes inside geometry or a single oversized probe for complex rooms. Ready to explore probe techniques and hands-on steps that you can apply in your next scene?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain the distinct roles of Light Probes and Reflection Probes, and implement them correctly in a baked scene. You will create and configure a Light Probe Group so dynamic objects inherit baked indirect lighting through interpolated probe samples. You will also set up Reflection Probes, choosing types and resolutions appropriate for interior and outdoor scenes, and tune influence volumes so reflections remain localized and accurate. Each objective ties to a practical skill: placing probe points at varying heights and transitions, re-baking lighting after placement, and using blend distances for smooth reflection transitions. For example, you will configure a metallic sphere to use a baked reflection probe so it shows the room’s cubemap rather than a generic skybox. We'll emphasize common mistakes like probes inside geometry, using too few probes, or relying on a single large probe for complex rooms. These pitfalls reduce realism or force expensive realtime updates. Mastering these objectives helps you produce believable visuals while keeping memory and bake-time costs manageable. Think of probes as the bridge between performance and photorealism: place and tune them smartly and the scene will read as cohesive and responsive.

This second objectives screen focuses on practical checks you can run in a scene. You will implement a Light Probe Group and verify dynamic objects use Blend Probes in their mesh renderer so they sample the interpolated ambient data. You will practice duplicating and moving individual probe points to refine coverage near doors, corners, and varying heights, then rebake to capture the updated samples. For Reflection Probes you will set type and resolution, adjust the box size to match the room, and use blend distance to smooth transitions between overlapping probes. For every change, learn to observe the effect: move a metallic sphere or your character and watch how lighting and reflections shift. This helps you spot mistakes like probes placed inside geometry or relying on a single oversized reflection probe that produces parallax errors. These skills keep your visuals accurate while avoiding excessive memory or bake-time costs. As you practice, ask: does the character pick up nearby color tints, and do reflections change plausibly when moving between rooms? Those checks confirm correct probe placement and configuration.

Light Probes are invisible sample points that capture the baked indirect light at a position so dynamic objects can receive believable ambient illumination. In concrete terms, Unity stores a small set of lighting coefficients at each probe. When a dynamic mesh moves through the scene, Unity interpolates the lighting from the nearest probes to determine the indirect diffuse contribution applied to that mesh. For example, if your character walks from a warm-lit corridor into a cooler shadowed room, properly placed probes ensure the character picks up the warm orange tint near the corridor and the softer blue-gray in the room. A common misconception is that Light Probes provide full, per-pixel global illumination for dynamic objects. They do not; probes provide an interpolated ambient sample, not full GI. Another mistake is treating probes like geometry: never place them inside walls or inside floors, because they sample from their local open space. To use probes, create a Light Probe Group, edit its probe positions at varying heights and near surfaces, and re-bake lighting so each probe stores the correct indirect data. Key takeaway: Light Probes bridge baked static lighting and dynamic objects with lightweight interpolated samples, preserving the visual connection between moving and static elements without realtime GI cost. How might you change probe density when a character can jump between floors?

Creating an effective Light Probe Group is a deliberate process: create the group, edit probes, place them to cover expected dynamic movement, and rebake lighting so probes store the sampled data. Start by adding a Light Probe Group, which provides an initial grid you can edit. Enter the probe edit mode and move individual probes: spread them near doorways, in corners, and at differing heights to capture vertical variations. A useful rule of thumb is to place probes near surfaces that contribute color bounces, like a red wall or glossy floor, and to ensure probes sit in open space rather than inside mesh. Duplicate probes to extend coverage along expected paths. After placement, generate lighting so the probes capture baked indirect light. Watch the results by moving a non-static object through the scene. If you see abrupt lighting shifts, add probes near the problematic transition rather than increasing probe density uniformly. A common misconception is that more probes always equal better results; instead, focus probes where lighting changes and use fewer probes in uniform areas to balance memory and bake time. This workflow helps you achieve smooth lighting interpolation while keeping resource use reasonable.

After placing initial probes you’ll refine coverage by selecting individual probes, moving them, or duplicating to fill gaps. Use the engine’s edit mode to pick specific probes and nudge them near surfaces or along movement paths. When refining, ask whether additional probes solve localized transitions or whether their benefit would be marginal; add probes only where lighting changes noticeably. Once satisfied with placement, rebake your lighting. Baking is crucial: Light Probes do not automatically sample updated indirect light until you generate lighting, so a common error is changing probe positions and forgetting to bake, which leaves probes with stale samples. For verification, place a non-static test object — for instance a capsule or player rig — and move it across probe regions. Observe subtle color shifts and brightness changes. If lighting pops, inspect probe placement near the popping boundary and add a probe to smooth interpolation. Keep balance in mind: too many probes increase memory and bake time, too few cause artifacts. The final step is to ensure the dynamic object's Mesh Renderer uses Blend Probes so it will interpolate the nearby probe data automatically. What small change could you make if your test object still looks too flat after rebaking?

A frequent challenge is balancing probe count against memory and bake-time cost. Too few probes cause visible popping and abrupt lighting changes on dynamic objects. Too many probes increase memory usage and lengthen bake times without a proportionate visual gain. Compare two approaches: a sparse uniform grid versus targeted placement. A sparse grid may miss transitions and color bounces, while targeted placement focuses probes at doorways, corners, and heights where dynamic objects move. A common misconception is that simply increasing total probes across the whole scene will always improve result; instead, prioritise probes where lighting changes. Another mistake is placing probes inside geometry or embedded in meshes; probes must sit in open space to sample the correct ambient light. For reflections, many artists try using a single large Reflection Probe for a big scene; this produces parallax errors and inaccurate reflections far from the probe center. Better is multiple smaller probes with overlapping blend distances to localize reflections and maintain geometric plausibility. The right balance keeps visuals realistic while controlling resource cost. Ask yourself: where does the player actually move, and where will reflections and light transitions be noticed most?

Reflection Probes capture a panoramic snapshot of a point in your scene and store that environment as a cubemap texture. That cubemap is then sampled by reflective materials to show environment reflections that match the local surroundings. Reflection Probes are essential for metallic surfaces, glossy plastics, water, and glass. There are three common probe types: baked, realtime, and custom. Baked probes capture a static cubemap during the lighting bake and are typically used for interiors where the environment doesn't change. Realtime probes update dynamically and can reflect moving objects or changing skies, but they are expensive and should be used sparingly. Custom probes let you assign a pre-made cubemap. Another key concept is the influence volume: the probe only affects objects within its box size and offset. When multiple probes overlap, use blend distance to smooth transitions so reflections change gradually between probe regions. A typical mistake is relying on a single probe for a large, complex area — this yields inaccurate parallax and unrealistic reflections far from the probe center. The correct approach is to localize probes and control blend distances so reflections remain convincing.

Reflection Probes come with several properties you must tune deliberately. Type determines how the cubemap is produced: Baked captures a static snapshot during the lighting bake and is the usual choice for static interiors. Realtime updates frames or at intervals and is reserved for special cases like mirrors or dynamic vehicles because it has a high runtime cost. Custom allows assignment of an authored cubemap. Resolution sets cubemap sharpness: higher resolution yields crisper reflections but consumes texture memory and increases bake or generation time. Box Size and Box Offset define the probe's influence volume — objects within that box sample the probe; objects outside do not. If probes overlap, Blend Distance smooths the transition so reflections interpolate rather than switch abruptly. For Realtime probes the Refresh Mode controls when cubemaps update, for example every frame or only on specific events; choose lower-frequency refreshes to save performance. A typical approach is to use baked probes per room with resolution around 128–256, and add smaller probes for specific reflective hotspots. Ask: does the visual improvement justify the memory and performance cost of a higher-resolution or realtime probe?

Good reflection placement is about localization and smooth blending. Place a reflection probe where reflections matter most — the center of a room, near water, or close to clusters of metallic objects. For large, complex rooms, distribute multiple smaller probes rather than a single large one; this avoids parallax errors where reflections appear geometrically wrong far from the probe center. When probe volumes overlap, use Blend Distance to interpolate between their cubemaps, creating a smooth transition. Too small a blend distance causes abrupt reflection changes; too large may blur localized detail. A practical sequence: place probes to cover each distinct sub-region, set box sizes to cover the relevant surfaces, then adjust blend distances to smooth transition zones like doorways. Validate by moving a reflective object across the overlap and noting whether reflections change gradually. A frequent misconception is that perfect geometric parallax requires realtime cubemaps; often, well-placed baked probes with smart blending give convincing results at lower cost. In short: localize, overlap thoughtfully, and fine-tune blend distance to maintain both realism and performance. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.
